4.0.0.en: The enemies of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, who lived near them, heard that they had founded the temple and were trying to complete its building. They feared for themselves lest the Jews gain power and drive them out of their land or do them harm. So they made plans and plots to stop the building of the temple and to limit the strength of those returning from captivity.

4.0.1.en: These enemies were the remnants of the ten tribes of Israel who lived in Samaria and its surroundings and mixed with the pagans whom the Assyrians had transferred and settled in the region of Samaria. These moved during the period of the Babylonian captivity and settled north of Jerusalem on the border of the kingdom of Judah, since the land was empty and its inhabitants were few.

4.0.2.en: The creed of these Samaritans was a mixture of the worship of God and belief in the books of Moses with the worship of the two golden calves, that is, the idols that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up after the split from the tribe of Judah and Jerusalem. To this was added the worship of the pagan gods of the pagans living with them, and we find their story in (2 Kgs 17). Therefore they were more dangerous to the people of God than the pagans, since they had the appearance of being Jews and worshiping God, although in truth they worshiped God as one of the gods and worshiped with Him the rest of the gods of the nations. Here the Jews are spoken of as the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, because most of those returning were from Judah and Benjamin and were able to prove their genealogies, whereas the rest of the tribes had been scattered and had forgotten their genealogies.

4.1.0.en: Esarhaddon: an Assyrian king who reigned from 681 to 669 BC. His policy was to remove the original inhabitants of a land and settle them in other places throughout his kingdom, in order to wipe out the nationality of these inhabitants so that they would all be citizens of the Assyrian kingdom, thus securing their submission. Accordingly he transferred pagans to the land of Samaria, and they mixed with the Jews who had split off from the tribe of Judah, that is, the ten tribes, and they worshiped God along with them together with the rest of the pagan gods.

4.1.1.en: The Samaritans who lived near Jerusalem came forward and asked Zerubbabel and the elders of Judah to let them share with them in building the house of God, whom their fathers had worshiped since the days of Esarhaddon's transfer of them from their lands to the region of Samaria. They declared that they were Jews, like the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, and therefore they had the right to build the house of the Lord. This was deceit and a means of stopping the building of the temple, because they worshiped God as one of the gods, did not keep the rites of His worship, and wished to place the statues of their pagan gods beside Him in His temple, and if those returning from captivity resisted them, they would stop the building.

4.1.2.en: The deceit and pride of these Samaritans appeared when those returning from captivity refused to let them share in the building, so they opposed them openly, as in the following verses. Thus the malice and evil of their hearts appeared, and in this they are like Judas Iscariot, about whom the Psalm prophesied (Ps 55:21).

4.2.0.en: Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the elders of Israel answered with one heart and in a decisive decision, and said to the Samaritans that the order of King Cyrus was for us alone, that we might build the house of the Lord, so it is not right for you to share with us in building it. God had revealed to them the deceit and trickery of the enemies, and they understood that they were not Jews like them, worshiping God alone. In this they showed that there is no fellowship of righteousness with iniquity, or of the people of God with the pagans.

4.3.0.en: After the people of God refused to let the pagans, the people of the land, that is, the Samaritans, share with them in the building, they showed their evil toward the people of God and began a series of plots to stop the building, for they knew that it was easier for them to stop the building from within than to stop it by an armed attack or by a royal order. Among these plots were:

4.3.1.en: 1- An attempt to weaken the resolve of the Jews, so that they would grow lazy about building the house of God and be distracted from its worship.

4.3.2.en: 2- When the attempt to make the people of God grow lazy about building failed, they resorted to a second means, which was to frighten the Jews, that is, to spread panic and terror in their hearts, whether by saying that the nations would rise against them, or that the king would be angry with them, or that wild beasts would attack them... But by the grace of God His people remained firm in faith and completed the building of the temple.

4.3.3.en: 3- Finally they resorted to a third means, which was to hire counselors within the royal court of King Cyrus, hoping to find a pretext or a reason to stop the building, and they paid many bribes. But the attempts of these counselors failed throughout the reign of Cyrus, and they continued these bribes to the counselors of the Persian king, not only in the days of Cyrus but also in the days of his son Cambyses, who is also called Artaxerxes, and until the reign of Darius, who reigned in 521 BC. Unfortunately Cambyses (Artaxerxes) responded to the wicked counselors, but Darius did not respond to them (you may consult the chronological table of the kings of Persia found in the introduction to this book).

4.3.4.en: Be firm in your faith however much the plots of the wicked surround you, and God will not allow any harm to come to you except what benefits you, and He will be with you and support you. Be confident and assured that your God, the Almighty, will never leave you.

4.4.0.en: The enemies of the people of God also resorted to official complaints which they sent to the kings of Persia. They may have begun in the days of Cyrus, but he did not respond to them, and they continued after this for a long time; that is, they sent them to many of the kings of Persia, even sending a complaint in the days of Ahasuerus, who reigned later, between 486 and 465 BC, and who married Esther. But they were not able to submit complaints to the king after him, Artaxerxes Longimanus, because he loved the Jews and appointed Nehemiah as his cupbearer, and in his days he allowed Ezra to return to Jerusalem, followed by Nehemiah in the third return. All this shows how evil these enemies were, who were able at a certain time to stop the building of the temple, as we shall see in the following verses. And even after the Jews were able to complete the building of the temple in the days of Darius, they afterward resumed sending complaints, even in the days of Ahasuerus, the husband of Esther.

4.4.1.en: The word for complaint in the Hebrew language is "sitnah", from which the word "Satan" or the devil is taken, who is the accuser of the children of God. That is, these wicked men walked in the way of Satan to hinder the work of God. But God is stronger than they.

4.5.0.en: Ezra tells us of one of the complaints that were sent in the days of King Artaxerxes, who is also called Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, who reigned from 529 to 522 BC. This complaint was presented by three of the chiefs of the nations surrounding the people of God, and King Artaxerxes was influenced by it. The text of this letter is not mentioned in the Bible, like the complaint of Ahasuerus mentioned in (v. 6) and like the rest of the complaints that were sent to King Cyrus.

4.5.1.en: The letter of Bishlam and his companions was written in the Aramaic language and interpreted in Aramaic, that is, written in Aramaic letters and not in Persian letters or any other language. Ezra did not translate these letters from Aramaic into Hebrew, but wrote them as they were, and this shows Ezra's accuracy. The written texts of the complaints and letters in this chapter, up to the sixth chapter, are all written in the Aramaic language.

4.6.0.en: This is a new complaint written by a person well known among the nations named Rehum, whose office was chancellor, that is, the judge or governor on behalf of the Persian state of a region neighboring Jerusalem and Judea, and he was assisted by his scribe Shimshai.

4.6.1.en: Rehum wrote this complaint also to Artaxerxes, that is, King Cambyses.

4.7.0.en: Asnapper: He was most likely Ashurbanipal, one of the kings of Assyria, a powerful king who transferred many peoples from their lands to other lands, among them the region of Samaria, which lies north of Jerusalem, and he reigned from 668 to 626 BC. This complaint was sent by Rehum and Shimshai, mentioned previously in (v. 8), and a great number of the peoples living in the region of Samaria, who had been transferred from distant lands in the kingdom of Assyria, allied themselves with them, so their names were written after the name of Rehum at the beginning of this letter. This was to show the importance and gravity of the complaint, that many had agreed upon it or signed it, and this also shows how evil these enemies were and their attempt to stir up King Artaxerxes against the Jews. Then they completed the rest of the usual introduction in glorifying kings, saying "and so forth."

4.8.0.en: Rehum and his companions showed their submission to King Artaxerxes in their complaint and made it known to him that they were his servants living in the region beyond the river, that is, the region lying west of the Euphrates river, which includes the region of present-day Syria and Palestine as far as the Mediterranean.

4.9.0.en: The complaint contained false accusations and left out important facts, in order to make Jerusalem appear in a bad light, and it included the following:

4.9.1.en: 1- The enemies accused the Jews who had gone up from Babylon to Jerusalem of building Jerusalem, the rebellious city, although it was a city subject to kings; but they exploited the rebellion of the last king of Judah, King Zedekiah, against Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chr 36:13), so Nebuchadnezzar seized him, took Jerusalem and destroyed it.

4.9.2.en: 2- They also accused the Jews of building the wall of Jerusalem and repairing the foundations of the city, and this did not happen until many years later in the days of Nehemiah, and it was by order of another king.

4.9.3.en: 3- They ignored the order of Cyrus, who asked Zerubbabel and the Jews with him to return and build the temple in Jerusalem.

4.9.4.en: 4- They claimed that the Jews would rebel against the king if they completed the walls, and would not pay tribute, which is the taxes collected from the citizens of the Persian state, nor custom, which is the tax collected on lands, nor toll, which is the tax collected for the Persian governor. All this accusation was false, for the Jews never rebelled against the Persian kings, even after the building of the temple and the walls of Jerusalem.

4.10.0.en: The enemies of the Jews showed their love and submission to the king by saying "we have maintenance from the king's palace", which means the king's favor to them, for he feeds them, since they receive their allowances from the king. So they showed their loyalty to the king and that they could not bear any harm coming upon the king. All this was of course lies, for they were wicked and did not want the greatness and strength of the Jews, fearing them, so they flattered the king to turn his heart against the Jews.

4.10.1.en: Thus we see in this chapter a series of steps in evil which these enemies took, namely:

4.10.2.en: 1- Deceit, by claiming that they wanted to help the Jews in the building (v. 2).

4.10.3.en: 2- Weakening the resolve of the people (v. 4).

4.10.4.en: 3- Frightening the people so that they would not complete the building (v. 4).

4.10.5.en: 4- Paying bribes to the counselors of the king of Persia so that they would speak evil of the Jews to the king (v. 5).

4.10.6.en: 5- Submitting complaints directly against the Jews (vv. 6-8).

4.10.7.en: 6- Flattering the king and showing their loyalty to him in order to stir him up against the Jews (v. 14).

4.10.8.en: 7- False accusations against the Jews, gathering any old faults of theirs, even from hundreds of years ago, calling Jerusalem the rebellious city (v. 15).

4.10.9.en: 8- Exploiting the Persians' love of collecting taxes to support their armies, by frightening them that if the Jews completed the building they would not pay taxes (v. 16).

4.11.0.en: The book of the records of thy fathers: the accounts of the kings and the events that accompanied them were written down in books kept in the government or in the palaces of the kings.

4.11.1.en: They accused the Jews of rebellion, relying on the rebellion of some kings such as King Manasseh, Ahaz, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, although the Jews returning from captivity were in complete submission to the state. Jerusalem had been destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, but the Jews did not present a harm to the state in general in their ancient generations, or in the recent generations, that is, after the return from captivity, when they were in utmost submission.

4.12.0.en: They threatened the king that when the building of Jerusalem and its walls was completed, it would certainly refuse to pay taxes, although this was a lie and did not happen.

4.12.1.en: Satan always stirs up the wicked to flatter and fawn upon rulers and to accuse the innocent falsely, as happened with Christ and happens to this day with the children of God.

4.12.2.en: Accept the false accusations and seek the counsel of God, and He will defend you. Know that Christ your Lord endured many false accusations for your sake, and be sure that He protects you and will make your right appear at the proper time.

4.13.s.en: (3) The stopping of the building of the temple

4.13.0.en: King Cambyses (Artaxerxes) answered the letter of Rehum and Shimshai and their companions with a message in which he first gave them peace, although the king's letter was full of evil against the Jews and in support of the evil of the Jews' enemies. The king had been drawn into the way of evil, but he offers peace as a customary word that does not carry its meaning.

4.14.0.en: The king said that the letter of Rehum had been plainly read before him, although Rehum had written it in Aramaic and then it was translated into Persian for the king to understand. He did not examine it carefully to know whether Rehum was harboring evil toward others or speaking with simplicity of heart. The king was deceived by the words of hypocrisy and praise that Rehum spoke, and he appears to understand everything while he understood nothing.

4.15.0.en: The king ordered his assistants to search the records kept by the king concerning the Jews, and they found, as he said, the following:

4.15.1.en: 1- Jerusalem is a city that rebels against kings and revolts against them.

4.15.2.en: 2- Mighty kings ruled over Jerusalem, who had their standing and whose power was feared.

4.15.3.en: 3- The kings of Jerusalem were strong and paid great taxes to the empire, and therefore the submission of this city is important so that the empire may receive taxes from them.

4.15.4.en: We must notice the presence of wicked, bribed counselors working for the king. When they searched for the accounts of the Jews, they were certain to look for proofs that condemned the Jews, and they would of course hide the order of Cyrus, who had commanded the return of the Jews from captivity and the building of the temple.

4.15.5.en: The search of the ancient documents showed that the kings of Jerusalem paid taxes, and this is positive evidence in favor of Jerusalem. But the king, because his assistants had stirred him up against Jerusalem, considered this matter alarming, since it was possible that Jerusalem would refuse to pay taxes.

4.15.6.en: The king's assistants who searched gathered the complaints that Rehum had sent since the days of Cyrus, all of them false complaints and false accusations, and presented them to the king as documents against Jerusalem. This is the habit of Satan, to bring logical proofs for his claims against the children of God. But whoever prays and examines calmly discovers the truth.

4.16.0.en: The king ordered the building to be stopped, and in this he fell into the error of contradicting the order of Cyrus his father, though it is not right to cancel a royal order, for the law of kings is not repealed (Dan 6:8). But the mercy of God appears in the king's order to stop the building in the following:

4.16.1.en: 1- The stopping was for a time until another order should be issued by the king, and was not a final stopping.

4.16.2.en: 2- The king did not order the demolition of what had been built.

4.16.3.en: 3- He did not punish those who had done the building, nor send them back into captivity.

4.16.4.en: God permitted the order to stop the building to be issued for the following reasons:

4.16.5.en: 1- The heart of the Jews was not complete in caring for the building of the temple, as shown by their being occupied, after the building of the temple was stopped, with building their own houses, so God sent the prophets Haggai and Zechariah to alert the people to the importance of building the temple of God.

4.16.6.en: 2- So that those returning from captivity might feel the importance of building the temple when its building was stopped, and then, after a period, it was permitted through the alert and prayers of those who love God. What comes easily is lost easily, but what a man obtains with labor he keeps with great care.

4.17.0.en: The weakness of King Artaxerxes appeared when he implored Rehum and those with him in his letter to carry out the order, so that no harm would come to him, especially since at the same time some skirmishes had broken out from the Greeks, whose aim was to seize some cities in Syria that were subject to his empire.

4.18.0.en: Rehum and his companions rejoiced at the king's letter, which contained the stopping of the building of the temple, and hastened with forces of soldiers and stopped the building in Jerusalem and showed them the king's order. They carried out the order quickly because it agreed with their evil desire, and not out of love for the king.

4.19.0.en: The building of the temple stopped as a result of the order of King Artaxerxes, and that was about the year 530 BC, and the stoppage continued until the second year of the reign of Darius, which is the year 520 BC, that is, it stopped for about ten years.

4.19.1.en: The Bible does not state that in this period the people grieved, prayed or fasted; rather they cared for building their own houses and were so occupied with them that they needed someone to awaken them spiritually, so God sent Haggai and Zechariah, who rebuked them for abandoning the building of the temple of God. It appears that the king's order stopped them, but the truth is that their heart was not concerned with completing the building of the temple. They had begun well when they set up the altar and laid the foundations of the temple, but they grew slack. So when the king's order to stop came, the Jews accepted it quietly because it agreed with their inward slackness. But when they were awakened spiritually, God bestowed on them not only the building of the temple but also its dedication, then the building of the walls of Jerusalem and their dedication, although this took time, so that their faith and steadfastness in God might be perfected. It was accomplished about seventy-five years after the year 520 BC, from the rebuilding of the temple until 445 BC at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem.

4.19.2.en: May you be with God with all your heart when you pray or do any good work, and if troubles come upon you, hold fast to your prayers, and the problem will be solved, and in any case your spiritual growth increases in both ease and distress. The return to the building of the temple

4.19.3.en: 1- The building of the temple of God began by order of King Cyrus in 535 BC, one year after his return from captivity, and continued for five years until the death of Cyrus in 530 BC, and his son Artaxerxes (Cambyses) became king, to whom the enemies of the people of God were able to complain about the Jews, so he issued an order to stop the building. It stopped for about ten years, until 520 BC, which is the second year of King Darius.

4.19.4.en: 2- We see in this chapter how the people grew slack and the Jews became occupied with building their own houses, so God sent them two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, who encouraged them, and they began building the temple, and God supported them, so the complaint of the civil governors of the region did not hinder them, as we shall see in this chapter.
